lessons.title: पाणी (pāṇī) — the first thing you'll actually ask for
lessons.gloss: water — the first thing you would actually ask for, and the request pattern that opens a spine node this track had never realized

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page

segments.text: आवडणे told you what you like; प्रेम करणे what you love. This chapter asks for something smaller and more frequent than either: a drink.
पाणी — pāṇī — water.
Nothing new here. प pa you have from punhā; ण you have from every -णे verb so far; ी is the familiar long ī. पा-णी.
पाणी, कृपया. — pāṇī, kṛpayā. — Water, please.

कृपया kṛpayā is Sanskrit's own instrumental of कृपा kṛpā, "mercy, kindness" — literally "by kindness, out of kindness." Name the thing you want, add कृपया, and the request is complete: no verb for "give" required. This is the pattern the whole chapter reuses, and the first time this track has built a "please" of any kind — a spine node this book had left empty until now.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — the oldest drinking word you own

segments.text: पाणी continues Maharastri Prakrit pāṇīa, from Sanskrit पानीय pānīya, "that which is to be drunk," built on पा pā-, "to drink." That root is Indo-European peh₃(i)-, and English keeps two disguised pieces of it: potion and poison both come through Latin potare, "to drink" — a poison, by origin, is just a drink gone wrong. Greek turned the same idea into sympotēs, "one who drinks together," which English keeps as symposium.

segments.instruction: malā marāṭhī āvaḍte, then pāṇī, kṛpayā — liking and requesting, side by side
segments.source: [YOU RUN: **malā marāṭhī āvaḍte**, then **pāṇī, kṛpayā** — liking and requesting, side by side]

segments.text: Ask for water politely. (Pāṇī, kṛpayā.) What does कृपया literally mean? ("By kindness.") Which two English words for a drink, and one for a whole gathering of them, share pāṇī's root? (Potion, poison, symposium.)
Sources: Wiktionary: पाणी (pāṇī); Wiktionary: कृपया.

lessons.title: चहा (chahā) — a word that took the overland road
lessons.gloss: tea — the one request in this chapter that is not inherited at all, and Marathi's first masculine noun

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: पाणी, कृपया (pāṇī, kṛpayā) — water, please. Say it once more, then ask for something that is not water at all.
चहा — chahā — tea.
चहा, कृपया. — chahā, kṛpayā. — Tea, please.
Nothing new. च you already say near ts from Chapter 9's चार; ह is नमस्कार's; ा the familiar long ā. Cha-hā.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — the one word in this chapter with no Sanskrit in it

segments.text: Every other word in this chapter reaches back to Sanskrit. चहा (chahā) does not — it is a loanword from Mandarin cha, and it reached Marathi by the overland route, through Persian and Turkic trade, the same road that gave Hindi चाय chāy, Bengali cha, and Persian chāy their words for the same drink. A second branch of the same plant travelled by sea: Dutch traders carried the Hokkien word te to Western Europe, which is why English says tea, not cha. One plant, two words, two trade routes.
चहा (chahā) is also this chapter's first masculine noun, against पाणी (pāṇī)'s neuter — a reminder that Marathi's three genders do not sort words by where they came from.

segments.instruction: the two trade routes — overland to chāy/chahā, by sea to tea
segments.source: [YOU NAME: the two trade routes — overland to *chāy/chahā*, by sea to *tea*]

segments.instruction: both requests — pāṇī, kṛpayā … chahā, kṛpayā
segments.source: [YOU SAY: both requests — **pāṇī, kṛpayā … chahā, kṛpayā**]

segments.text: Ask for tea politely. (Chahā, kṛpayā.) Which language does चहा (chahā) ultimately come from? (Mandarin Chinese, cha.) Which English word for the same plant took the sea route instead? (Tea.)
Sources: Wiktionary: चहा (chahā).

lessons.title: दूध (dūdh) — back to Sanskrit, and a surprising English cousin
lessons.gloss: milk — back to inherited Sanskrit, and the same PIE root behind English doughty

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: चहा (chahā) broke the pattern — a loanword with no Sanskrit behind it. This next word rejoins पाणी (pāṇī)'s family: inherited, traceable, Indo-European.
दूध — dūdh — milk.
दूध, कृपया. — dūdh, kṛpayā. — Milk, please.
One new mark: ू, the long ū vowel sign — a longer hook under the consonant than any you've written so far. द you have from dhanyavād and madat; ध from dhanyavād too. Dū-dh.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — milk, and the root behind "doughty"

segments.text: दूध (dūdh) continues Maharastri Prakrit duddha, from Sanskrit दुग्ध dugdha, "milked, milk" — literally the past participle of दुह् duh-, "to milk." That root traces to Indo-European dʰewgʰ-, "to be fit, to be of use, to produce" — milking as producing something useful. Germanic kept the same root for a different sense of "useful, capable": English doughty, "brave and able," is dūhtig in Old English, built on this exact root. Milk and doughtiness, four thousand years apart, share one ancestor.

segments.instruction: all three requests — pāṇī, chahā, dūdh — kṛpayā
segments.source: [YOU RUN: all three requests — **pāṇī, chahā, dūdh** — kṛpayā]

segments.text: Ask for milk politely. (Dūdh, kṛpayā.) What English word for "brave and capable" shares दूध (dūdh)'s root? (Doughty.)
Sources: Wiktionary: दूध (dūdh).

lessons.title: भाकरी (bhākarī) — the request that breaks the pattern
lessons.gloss: a round flatbread — the one word in this chapter that never left Marathi's own neighborhood, and Hindi's word for bread altogether

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Three requests so far: pāṇī, chahā, dūdh. Two inherited from Sanskrit, one borrowed from Chinese. The fourth belongs to neither story.
भाकरी — bhākarī — a round flatbread, the everyday Maharashtrian bread — of jowar, bajra, or rice flour, not wheat.
भाकरी, कृपया. — bhākarī, kṛpayā. — Bhakri, please.
Nothing new. भ from bheṭū, क from everywhere, र from marāṭhī, ी the familiar long ī. Bhā-ka-rī.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — the one word that stayed home

segments.text: भाकरी is inherited from Old Marathi bhākarī, from Proto-Indo-Aryan bʰakkaras, "heap, pile, lump" — the flatbread named for the lump of dough it started as. That reconstruction is as far back as the sources trace it; its own root before Proto-Indo-Aryan is not established, so this lesson claims none rather than inventing one.

Unlike पाणी (pāṇī) and दूध (dūdh), भाकरी (bhākarī) is not a Sanskrit tatsama or tadbhava — it never touched classical Sanskrit. And unlike चहा (chahā), it is no loanword either — a regional word, close kin to Gujarati bhākhrī and Kannada bakkari, and simply not Hindi's word for bread: Hindi asks for रोटी roṭī, an unrelated root. A Delhi shopkeeper would not recognize the request; a Pune one would hand you lunch.

Say the four requests once more and notice their genders: पाणी (pāṇī) neuter, चहा (chahā) masculine, दूध (dūdh) neuter, भाकरी (bhākarī) feminine. Four everyday nouns, all three of Marathi's genders, in one short chapter — proof, alongside the verbs' present-tense endings, that the third gender Hindi lost is not a museum piece here.

segments.source: [YOU NAME: which of the four is neither Sanskrit nor a loanword — **bhākarī**]

segments.text: What did भाकरी's Proto-Indo-Aryan ancestor mean? (A heap, a lump.) What does Hindi ask for instead? (रोटी, an unrelated root.) Give all four requests with their genders. (पाणी (pāṇī) n, चहा m, दूध n, भाकरी f — all with कृपया.) Sort the four sources: two from Sanskrit, one a Chinese loan, one purely regional. (Pāṇī, dūdh — Sanskrit; chahā — Chinese; bhākarī — regional.)
